newsitem.title: CHINA: China mulls allowing banks to set debt structure.
newsitem.headline: China mulls allowing banks to set debt structure.

text.p: China is considering allowing financial institutions autonomy in adjusting their foreign debt structure, but within government-set ceilings, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday.

The relaxation would apply to designated foreign exchange banks and financial institutions with foreign borrowing rights, the newspaper quoted an official of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange as saying.

Institutions would be allowed autonomy in adjusting their debt structure as long as they kept long and medium-term foreign debt within a ceiling and met the central bank's asset-liabilities ratio, he said.
Long and medium-term debt referred to foreign loans, leasing and overseas bonds of at least one-year terms.
Most institutions welcomed the reform, aimed at reducing risk and using funds more efficiently, the official said.
While drafting of the new rules was expected to be finished by the end of the year, implementation must await approval by the State Council, or cabinet, he said.

At present, the State Planning Commission sets foreign debt quotas for large construction projects that rely on financial institutions for foreign funds, but this has resulted in some problems, the official said.

For example, the construction and investment yields of such projects take longer than the foreign debt terms, which leaves the financial institutions unable to recall the funds to repay foreign debt on time.
Under the existing system, financial institutions also fail to select the best interest rate and term for foreign borrowing according to the market.

Since the state-set foreign debt quotas are valid only for a limited period, institutions sometimes borrow money to avoid wasting their quotas even though the market is not favourable, the official said.
"Our foreign debt management should go to the market and give some autonomy to financial institutions," he said.

Such an experiment since 1992 with the China International Trust and Investment Corp (CITIC) had proved successful, with CITIC's outstanding foreign debt dropping to $2.3 billion last year from $2.5 billion in 1992, he said. Last year, the government gave CITIC a five-year extension of its autonomy.
